title: What is a training needs analysis?
description: A training needs analysis (TNA) finds the gap between required and current capability and decides what training closes it. Levels, steps and an example.
shortAnswer: A training needs analysis (TNA) is a structured process for identifying the gap between the capability an organization, role or person needs and the capability they currently have, and for deciding whether training is the right way to close it. A good TNA ends with prioritized, evidence based training requirements linked to specific roles, risks and obligations, not a wish list of courses.
keyTakeaways: A TNA compares required capability (from a competency framework, obligations or strategy) with current capability, then decides how to close the gap.
Analysis is usually done at three levels: organization, job or task, and individual.
Not every gap is a training gap: poor tools, unclear procedures or workload can look like missing skills.
In regulated work, a TNA is the documented reasoning that shows why training was, or was not, provided for each obligation.

sections.heading: How does a training needs analysis work?

blocks.text: A training needs analysis works by defining what good performance requires, measuring what exists now, and analyzing the difference. The requirement side usually comes from a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework), a regulation or standard, a procedure, or a business strategy. The current state comes from assessment results, audit findings, incident data, supervisor observation and self assessment.

A classic TNA examines needs at [three levels: organization, job task and individual](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/money-business/workplace-learning-coaching-and-mentoring/content-section-1.1). The levels answer different questions, and skipping one tends to produce training that is either unfocused or disconnected from strategy.

Who has the gap, and how large is it?

sections.heading: Where is training needs analysis used?

blocks.text: Training needs analysis is a recognized task in quality standards and national vocational systems. ISO 9001 clause 7.2, for example, requires an organization to determine the competence its people need, act to close gaps and evaluate whether the action worked ([ISO 9001 competence requirements](/regulations/iso-9001-competence-requirements)).

Regulators also expect training decisions to be reasoned. In Portugal, employers must give each worker adequate safety and health training that takes account of their workstation and any high risk activities ([Portugal OHS training requirements](/regulations/portugal-ohs-training-requirements)). In Australian mining, the NSW Resources Regulator links [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) to the duty to provide information, training and instruction in clause 39 of the NSW Work Health and Safety Regulation 2017 ([NSW Resources Regulator](https://www.resources.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-05/operating-mobile-plant-verification-of-competency.pdf)). A TNA is how an employer shows that training was matched to the work.

sections.heading: How is a training needs analysis different from a gap analysis?

blocks.text: A TNA asks what training is needed and for whom; a training gap analysis usually asks whether existing training covers what it should. The two overlap and are often run together. The full comparison is in [training needs analysis vs gap analysis](/compare/training-needs-analysis-vs-gap-analysis).

items: A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) is often an output of a TNA: it records the training each role requires.
A [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) is one of the inputs: it measures current capability.
A curriculum or course design follows the TNA; it should not come first.

sections.heading: What does a training needs analysis look like in practice?

blocks.text: The following is an illustrative example for a health service introducing a revised medication handling procedure.

items: **Organization level:** the revised procedure is a clinical risk priority; the change must be embedded across three wards before an accreditation assessment.
**Task level:** compare the old and new procedure step by step. Four steps change; two of them are safety critical.
**Individual level:** a short scenario check with a sample of staff shows most understand two of the changes but not the other two.
**Cause check:** the two misunderstood steps rely on a new form that has not yet been distributed. That is a resourcing gap, not a training gap.
**Decision:** targeted training on the two safety critical steps for all nursing staff, a form rollout before training, and an observed practice check on each ward four weeks later.

blocks.text: The full method is in [how to conduct a training needs analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-training-needs-analysis).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records the required side of a TNA as a structured framework of obligations, concepts and assessment points. Comparing that framework with existing content and assessment results shows where gaps sit and which roles they affect.

faqs.q: How long does a training needs analysis take?
faqs.a: It depends on scope. A TNA for one procedure change can take days; an organization wide TNA covering many roles and obligations can take months. Scoping the analysis to the risks and roles that matter most, and reusing an existing competency framework, is the main way to keep it proportionate.

Usually a learning and development specializt working with the people who own the requirement, such as compliance, risk or operational managers, and with supervisors who can describe actual performance. Subject matter experts confirm what the task requires. The analyst's job is to keep the process evidence based and to separate training gaps from other causes.

faqs.q: What is the output of a training needs analysis?
faqs.a: A documented set of training requirements: which roles or people need what capability, to what standard, by when, and how it will be checked. It should also record gaps that training will not fix, with the reason, so decisions can be reviewed later. Many organizations turn the output into a training matrix and a training plan.

faqs.q: How often should a TNA be repeated?
faqs.a: Repeat it when a trigger occurs, such as a new regulation, a changed procedure, a new role, an incident or an audit finding, and on a regular planning cycle. Keeping the requirements linked to their sources makes it easier to rerun only the affected parts rather than the whole analysis.
